summary: A working paper from MIT Lincoln Laboratory on interprocess communication facilities. It argues that the goals are more complicated than commonly realized, and a satisfactory design must satisfy more than just moving bits between independent programs.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 150 argues that interprocess communication must do more than move bits between programs. It lists services processes may need, while warning that the paper is incomplete and does not propose a single implementation.

questions: what does interprocess communication need to handle
what does a process need to flow control messages
what services do processes need from ipc
subtitle: A working paper on the services processes need from interprocess communication.

tldr.problem: Moving bits between processes is not enough; an interprocess communication facility must support the processes' real input, output, timing and recovery needs.
tldr.mechanism: Richard Kalin describes usage patterns and desired services, including wakeup criteria, partial messages, buffer guarantees, channel status and error recovery.
tldr.outcome: The paper is explicitly incomplete and does not propose solutions, arguing that useful solutions must depend on the machine.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 150 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text is an explicitly incomplete working paper on the usage needs of interprocess communication.

sections.title: Communication Is More Than Moving Bits
sections.content:
Richard Kalin argues that interprocess communication (IPC) has more complex goals than moving bits between otherwise independent programs. An IPC design must meet the constraints created by how processes use it.

The paper is a working document based on limited experience with early IPC systems. The author says its list of usage patterns is incomplete and should not be treated as authoritative or final.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs need a communication system that fits how they work, not just one that passes data. The author presents these needs as an incomplete working list.

sections.title: When Processes Should Wake Up
sections.content:
A process may need a particular amount or kind of input before it can work efficiently, such as a complete character, line or file. Waking a process too early wastes system work, while waiting for too much input can create inefficiency or input deadlocks.

The paper discusses using a requested amount, a condition such as a carriage return, or a boundary supplied by the producer to decide when to wake a process. It calls the data between logical boundaries a logical message.
sections.plainLanguage: A process may need a complete unit of input before it can do useful work. The system needs ways to know when enough data has arrived without waking the process too often or waiting too long.

sections.title: Send and Receive Messages in Parts
sections.content:
A sending process may not have enough storage to prepare a whole logical message at once, so it should be able to send the message in parts and mark the final part. A receiving process may also lack room for a complete message and should be able to accept it in parts.

Partial reception is also needed for messages too large for system buffers. If the receiver cannot accept part of a message, transmission may never complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver may both have limited storage. The facility should let them transfer a long message in parts and identify when the final part arrives.

sections.title: Buffers, Channels and Recovery
sections.content:
The paper lists further needs: learn whether a message can be sent, reserve output buffer space, inspect outstanding or queued messages, get wakeups when queue conditions change, and distinguish message counts from bits as measures of channel capacity. It also discusses setting channel capacity limits and closing channels.

Other topics include transferring channel privileges, establishing channels, reporting transmission errors and letting a receiver reject a message so the system can use any internal recovery mechanism it has. The paper does not prescribe particular mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Processes may need to check buffer space, manage channels and learn when messages arrive or are accepted. The paper lists these needs but leaves implementation choices open.
